lesson.title: Reading a chemical formula

steps.headline: A subscript counts atoms in one unit, and a coefficient counts how many units.

lead.text: The small number after a symbol is a subscript. In H₂O it says there are two H atoms in each molecule, and no number means one.
A big number in front is a coefficient. It counts whole molecules: 2 H₂O is two molecules.
Look at the three water molecules and decide what to count.

reveal.text: You took the oxygen in one molecule and counted it once per molecule. That is what a coefficient asks for.

steps.headline: How many hydrogen atoms are in 4 H₂SO₄?

workedSteps.text: Read the subscript: each H₂SO₄ has 2 H atoms.
Read the coefficient: there are 4 units.
Multiply the atoms in one unit by the units.

steps.headline: Count the oxygen atoms in 2 Al₂O₃.

workedSteps.text: The subscript after O is 3, so each unit has 3 oxygen atoms.

steps.headline: Change a coefficient to change the amount. Changing a subscript changes the substance.

lead.text: Change H₂O to H₂O₂ and you have hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. To have more water without changing it, write a bigger number in front.
Add up the atoms of every element in one unit first, then multiply by the units.
Ammonia is NH₃. A missing subscript means one atom.

lesson.orientation: Separate subscripts inside a formula from coefficients multiplying whole units.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A sandwich box holds 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. You buy 5 boxes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the atoms of each element in something like 3 H₂O.

recap.keyIdea: A subscript counts the atoms of an element in one unit, and a coefficient counts the units. Multiply the two to count the atoms.

blocks.text: You counted hydrogen in 4 H₂SO₄, oxygen in 2 Al₂O₃ and every atom in 2 H₂SO₄. Each time you took the atoms in one unit and multiplied by the units.

recap.nextHook: Once you can count atoms, you can add up their masses. Next: the mass of one formula unit.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in 3 H₂O molecules?
hints: Multiply the O subscript, which is one, by the coefficient.
Each H₂O contains one O atom.
Each water contributes one oxygen; count the water molecules.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Each H₂O has one oxygen, and the coefficient says there are three of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen in one molecule. The coefficient multiplies it.
That counts the hydrogen as well. The question asks about oxygen.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 2 Al₂O₃ formula units?
hints: Multiply the entire formula by two.
The O subscript is three.
Multiply 2 formula units by 3 O atoms per unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unit has three O atoms: 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Each unit has three O atoms, and there are two units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen in one unit. There are more than one unit.
That adds the numbers. Atoms per unit and units multiply.

questions.prompt: To double an amount of water without changing the substance, what do you change?
hints: Keep the formula of each molecule fixed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A coefficient multiplies whole water molecules.

questions.onCorrect: The coefficient counts molecules, so double it. Changing a subscript would change the substance.

misconceptions.feedback: Changing a subscript changes the molecule itself, so it is no longer water.
Changing the element symbol makes a different substance.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 5 NH₃ molecules?
hints: Each ammonia molecule contributes three H atoms.
The H subscript is three.
Multiply 5 molecules by 3 H atoms per molecule.
questions.onCorrect: 15. Each NH₃ has three H atoms, and five molecules have five times as many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hydrogen in one molecule, not in all five.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the hydrogen in one molecule by the molecules.

questions.prompt: How many chlorine atoms are represented by 4 MgCl₂ formula units?
hints: Apply the coefficient to chlorine too.
The Cl subscript is two.
Multiply 4 formula units by 2 Cl atoms per unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unit contributes two Cl atoms: 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each MgCl₂ has two Cl atoms, and there are four units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chlorine in one unit. There are more than one unit.
That adds the numbers. Multiply them.

hints: Read the outside number separately from the inside number.

acceptedIdeas: Two molecules with two H atoms each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The coefficient counts molecules and the subscript counts atoms per molecule.

choices.label: One molecule with four bonded H atoms
Two molecules with two H atoms each

questions.onCorrect: The coefficient counts molecules and the subscript counts atoms in each, so 2 H₂ is two molecules of two atoms.

misconceptions.feedback: The 2 in front counts molecules, so it does not join the atoms into one molecule.
The atoms in each molecule are bonded, not isolated.

questions.prompt: How many slices of bread are in the 5 boxes?
hints: How much bread is in one box?
Each box has the same amount.
Multiply the bread in one box by the number of boxes.
questions.onCorrect: 10. One box's contents times the number of boxes. A formula with a number in front works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bread in one box. You bought more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the bread in one box by the boxes.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of CH₄?
hints: Find the small number after the H.
That is the subscript, and it counts that element's atoms.
There is one molecule, so nothing else multiplies it.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The subscript after H counts the hydrogen atoms in one molecule.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the carbon, which has no subscript. The question asks about hydrogen.
That counts every atom. The question asks about hydrogen only.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the subscript by the coefficient?

acceptedIdeas: The coefficient says how many units there are, and each unit has that many atoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms in one unit times the units gives all the atoms.

choices.label: The coefficient says how many units there are, and each unit has that many atoms
The subscript tells us the number of molecules

questions.onCorrect: Right: each unit has the same atoms, so the total is atoms per unit times units.

misconceptions.feedback: The subscript counts atoms in one unit. The coefficient counts units.
This is only counting atoms. Balancing is a different job.

questions.prompt: How many atoms of all elements are in 2 H₂SO₄?
hints: Add up the atoms of every element in one H₂SO₄ first.
Read the three subscripts, and remember S has none.
Multiply that total by the number of units.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One H₂SO₄ has 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms, so 2 units have 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Seven atoms in one unit, and two units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one unit's atoms. There are more than one unit.
That counts only the hydrogen and the oxygen. Include the sulfur.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 3 C₂H₆ molecules?
hints: Find the subscript after H.
That is the hydrogen in one molecule.
Multiply it by the molecules.
questions.onCorrect: 18. Six hydrogen atoms per molecule, three molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hydrogen in one molecule. There are more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the hydrogen in one molecule by the molecules.
